status.en: 21 armed incidents reported in the past seven days, 22% fewer than the week before, most of them in Tigray, Amhara and Addis Ababa.
status.nb: 21 væpnede hendelser meldt de siste sju dagene, 22 prosent færre enn uken før, flest i Tigray, Amhara og Addis Ababa.

summary.en: Ethiopian forces have seized a key town in Tigray that includes the regional airport and are moving toward an Eritrean border town, while fighting in Amhara has left at least 183 dead, according to the UN. Militia reports say Eritrean forces suffered losses as Ethiopian troops expand control in Tigray. The United States is urging Ethiopia and Eritrea to de-escalate, and the Ethiopian Red Cross condemned an attack that killed an ambulance driver in Benishangul-Gumuz. Hospitals in Tigray have resumed operations as supplies arrive, and the conflict caused 2,824 battle-related deaths in 2024, according to UCDP.
summary.nb: Etiopiske styrker har tatt kontroll over en viktig by i Tigray som inkluderer regionens flyplass og beveger seg mot en eritreisk grenseby, mens kampene i Amhara har etterlatt minst 183 døde, ifølge FN. Militsrapporter sier at eritreiske styrker led tap mens etiopiske tropper utvider kontrollen i Tigray. USA oppfordrer Etiopia og Eritrea til å de-eskalere, og den etiopiske Røde Kors fordømte et angrep som drepte en ambulansefører i Benishangul-Gumuz. Sykehus i Tigray har gjenopptatt driften etter at forsyninger ankommer, og konflikten forårsaket 2 824 dødsfall i kamper i 2024, ifølge UCDP.

background.title: Fano insurgency
background.extract: The Fano insurgency is an armed conflict and insurgency in the Amhara Region of Ethiopia that began in April 2023 between the Fano militia and the Ethiopian government. The conflict started after the government attempted to dissolve the Amhara Special Forces and other regional forces as part of a plan to reform and centralize the country's security apparatus, and integrate them into the federal armed forces. This move led to protests and armed resistance by local forces under Fano.
